notes.text: 写前分析的反转验证:事实 F09（疑似血迹）：如果真的是暴力事件，可能与'瞬间威胁'论点冲突。但处理方式：F09 的化验未能确认是暴力，且即使有冲突，也不能解释为什么所有人（包括2岁女儿）都上救生艇、为什么攻击者不拿货物。F09 加深谜团但不推翻'弃船决定致命'的核心论点——无论触发原因是什么，上救生艇这个应对方式本身就是死刑 和反转结论相反(F14（2026年乙醇闪燃理论）是关键补充，它解决了'为什么有紧急情况但船完好'的矛盾：闪燃可以产生巨大冲击（炸飞舱门、巨响）让船长以为船要爆炸/着火，但实际上几秒就结束、不会持续燃烧木材。这让论点从'没有理由弃船'升级为'有瞬间威胁但错误评估了持续性'，更符合人性、更有说服力)

CH01.text:
[CH01 | 0:00-0:50 | 第一秒场景落地，身份确立，阶层检查仪式，核心悬念抛出]

I'm a sailor on the Mary Celeste. It's November 1872, and I just signed on for a voyage to Italy. The ship is solid, the cargo is valuable, and the captain brought his wife and daughter. Everything seems fine. Except I know something no one else on this ship knows: in nine days, we're all going to be dead. Not because of a storm, not because of pirates. Because of a lifeboat.

How did I end up here? A man at the docks. A crimp. That's what they call them. He finds sailors for ships. He asks: how much do you owe? Do you have work on land? I need the money. He knows that. So I sign. The contract says I get forty dollars for this voyage. Two, maybe three months of wages, paid upfront. Sounds good. Until he tells me: that forty dollars? It's his fee. For finding me this job. I just signed on to work a transatlantic crossing for free.

That's who gets on ships like this. People who have no other choice.

There are ten of us on this ship. Captain Benjamin Briggs. His wife Sarah. Their two-year-old daughter. Seven crew. And in a few days, this ship is going to be found drifting in the middle of the Atlantic, 400 miles from land. Empty. No bodies. No struggle. Just gone.

Why would ten people abandon a perfectly good ship?

That's what I'm here to find out.

CH02.text:
[CH02 | 0:50-1:15 | 制作坦白，建立真实性契约]

Here's the thing. The Mary Celeste was found empty. No survivors to interview.

What you'll see—the quarters, the meals, the work—comes from the ship's log, 1870s merchant ship records, and vessels like this one.

We don't know exactly what happened. But we know they made a decision. And we know why it was deadly.

So what's my mission?

CH03.text:
[CH03 | 1:15-1:45 | 任务简报，挂出探索清单]

So what's my mission?

Three places. The captain's cabin—that's where the log is, the navigation charts, the decisions. The cargo hold—1,701 barrels of industrial alcohol down there. And the deck—where we work, where we'll be when it happens.

Ten people on this ship. Captain Briggs. His wife Sarah. Their two-year-old daughter. Seven crew, including me.

The ship's sound. Cargo's secured. Supplies are good.

So why does everyone abandon it?

That's what I need to find out. When did they decide? What made them think: we have to leave right now?

Because that decision—that one choice—kills all of us.

All right. Let's start where I sleep.

CH04.text:
[CH04 | 1:45-3:15 | 第1级：船员舱物理环境建立]

Okay. So this is where I sleep.

The fo'c'sle. Forward crew quarters.

It's dark down here. One small hatch. Lamp oil's rationed, so most of the time you're moving by feel.

The bunk's maybe five and a half feet long. I'm not tall—most sailors aren't—but my feet still hang off the end. You sleep curled up. Every night. For weeks.

Everything's damp. The walls sweat saltwater. Your blanket's damp. Your clothes are damp. You touch the wood and it's slick.

There's a smell. Tar. They use it to seal the hull, and it seeps through the planks. Mix that with saltwater and unwashed bodies and you've got the air down here.

And the rats.

You hear them in the walls at night. Scratching. Chewing. Sometimes one runs across the floor. You learn to ignore it.

Imagine sleeping in a youth hostel. Now make it smaller. Make it wet. Make it constantly moving—rolling, pitching, creaking. Add rats. Add the smell of tar and brine.

And you can't leave.

You signed the contract. New York to Genoa. Several weeks at sea. This bunk, this damp little space, is where you live until we get there.

I've stayed in worse places on land. But on land, you can walk out. Here, you're 400 miles from anything. The door at the top of those stairs leads to the deck. The deck leads to the ocean.

This is it.

The crew sleeps six to a cabin like this. Shoulder to shoulder. When one guy rolls over, everyone feels it.

Your trunk fits under the bunk. That's all the space you get. Everything you own: spare shirt, spare pants, maybe a book if you can read, your tobacco if you've got any.

At night, the ship rolls and you hear the cargo shifting in the hold below. Barrels creaking against their lashings. Ropes groaning. The whole structure of the ship flexing.

You get used to it. Or you don't sleep.

Right now, it's daytime. Most of the crew's on deck. I've got a few minutes before my watch.

So. That's the bunk. That's the air. That's the space.

What about food? What do we actually eat down here?

And who are these men I'm sleeping next to?

CH05.text:
[CH05 | 3:15-4:45 | 第1级：船员社会背景与经济处境]

Food.

Standard ration for a sailor in the 1870s: six pounds of bread per week. A pound and a half of salted beef per day, or a pound and a quarter of pork if the beef runs out. Hardtack biscuits. Water, three quarts a day if we're lucky.

The meat's been pickled in brine for months. It's tough. Salty. Sometimes you can't tell if it's beef or leather.

The hardtack? After a few weeks at sea, you check it for weevils before you bite. Little black holes in the biscuit. If you see them, you just break off that part. Or you don't, and you get the protein.

Not great. But I've had worse.

The men I'm bunking with—most of them signed on the same way I did. Through a crimp back in New York. Some guy on the docks who promised work, handed over a contract, and took two months' wages up front as his fee.

Forty dollars. Gone before you even step on the ship.

One of the guys in the bunk next to me, he's sailing to pay off a debt. Another one's hoping to start over in Europe. Get off in Genoa, find work, maybe send money back home.

We don't know exactly what they said to each other. No one recorded the conversations in the fo'c'sle. But sailors in the 1870s? This is what they talked about. Debts. Plans. The next port.

At dinner, someone asks what I'm going to do in Italy.

I don't have an answer.

These men do. They've got futures. They've got reasons for being here.

And in a few weeks, every single one of them is going to make the same decision.

So here's a question.

Is there any joy on this ship? Any moments where these men aren't just surviving?

CH06.text:
[CH06 | 4:45-6:15 | 第1级：船员社群与信念系统]

Yes. There is.

Evening on deck. The work's done. Someone's pulled out a deck of cards. Someone else has a tin whistle. Not a party. Just — time that's ours.

I'm terrible at cards. I lose three hands in a row and nobody cares.

There's a guy they call Old Thomas. Been at sea longer than I've been alive. He's watching the game, not playing. Just smoking his pipe.

He tells a story. A ship he was on in '58. Storm off Newfoundland. Captain wanted to run for shore. Thomas convinced him to ride it out.

"The ship knows," he says. "Forty years I've been sailing. You learn: when you're not sure, trust the ship. She'll tell you if she's really dying."

Everyone nods. Like it's gospel.

I need to remember that. I don't know why yet, but I need to remember it.

The music's bad. The jokes are worse. But nobody's checking my papers here. Nobody's asking if I paid my debt. We're just crew.

And here's the thing: I've been lying to all of them since the moment I got on board.

So I'm going to stop.

Thomas, can I tell you something?

He looks at me. Go ahead.

I'm not from 1872.

Long pause.

I'm from the future. 2026. I know what happens to this ship. I know it gets found empty. And I need to get into the captain's quarters to figure out why.

He stares at me for a long time.

Then he taps his pipe out on the rail.

"You're a strange one," he says. "But I've seen stranger things at sea."

He leans in.

"Captain does his night watch alone. Deck clears out around ten. You'll have maybe twenty minutes before the mate comes by."

That's it. That's all I needed.

I don't know if he believes me. Maybe he thinks I'm mad. Maybe he just likes a good story.

But he gave me the way in.

And tomorrow night, I'm going to take it.

CH07.text:
[CH07 | 6:15-7:45 | 第2级：信任交换与禁区通道获取]

All right. So I have my window.

Ten o'clock. Captain on deck. Twenty minutes.

That's when I go in.

The next day drags. Every watch feels twice as long. I'm running through it in my head: what I'm looking for, where it might be, how fast I need to move.

The ship's log. That's the first thing. November 25th was the last entry—I need to see what it says. Position, weather, anything unusual.

Then the cargo manifest. 1,701 barrels of alcohol. I need to know what condition they're in, if there's been any damage, any leaks.

And the charts. Where we are, where we're going, how far from land.

Because if something happens—when something happens—I need to understand what options they think they have.

The old sailor doesn't say anything to me all day. Just nods once when we pass on deck.

That night, I wait in my bunk. Listen to the others settle in. Someone's snoring. Someone else is whispering a prayer.

I slip out just after nine-thirty.

The deck is quiet. A few lanterns swinging in the rigging. The sound of water against the hull.

I can see the captain up near the bow, hands behind his back, looking out at nothing.

The companionway to his cabin is right there. Fifteen feet away.

I wait until he turns, starts pacing toward the stern.

Then I move.

Down the steps. My hand on the latch.

It opens.

I'm in.

The cabin is small. Smaller than I expected. A desk bolted to the floor. A narrow bed. Shelves lined with books, navigation tools, a sextant.

And on the desk: the logbook.

I flip it open. The handwriting is neat, precise.

November 25th. Position: approximately 110 miles west of Santa Maria, Azores. Weather clearing after rough seas. Course steady.

Nothing unusual. Nothing that explains why, days from now, this ship will be empty.

I check the cargo manifest next. It's clipped to a board hanging on the wall.

1,701 barrels. Industrial alcohol. Loaded in New York. Destination: Genoa.

Nine barrels marked with a note: "Found empty on inspection, contents evaporated or leaked, remainder secured."

Nine barrels out of 1,701. That's nothing. Cargo like this always has some loss.

But I can smell it. Even here, even with the door closed. That sharp, chemical smell. Stronger than it should be.

I'm about to check the charts when I hear footsteps on the deck above.

I freeze.

The mate. Early.

I close the logbook, hang the manifest back exactly where it was.

I slip out, back up the companionway, and I'm halfway across the deck when the mate appears.

He looks at me. I look at him.

"Couldn't sleep," I say.

He grunts. Doesn't care.

I go back below.

And I lie there in my bunk, staring at the ceiling.

I got in. I got what I needed.

The ship's log says everything is fine. The cargo manifest says everything is fine.

But I know what happens next.

And I still don't know why.

CH08.text:
[CH08 | 7:45-9:05 | 第2级：决策者私人空间与家庭]

The next night, I go back.

The captain's on deck. The mate's forward. I slip into the cabin.

And it's different.

Not grand. Nothing like what you'd imagine on a passenger ship.

But clean. Organized. A proper desk, a proper chair. Navigation instruments mounted on the wall — sextant, chronometer, charts rolled and labeled. Everything has a place.

The air smells different too. Not tar and sweat. Wood polish. Lamp oil.

And then I see the other things.

A woman's shawl, folded on the back of a chair. A small hand mirror on the desk. A hairbrush.

His wife is here.

Sarah.

I knew that. I knew the captain brought his family.

But knowing it and seeing her things — it's different.

There's a narrow bunk on the starboard side, made up with a quilt. Not regulation issue. Something from home.

And on the shelf above it — a wooden toy. A little horse, hand-carved. Paint worn off on one side.

For a two-year-old.

I stand there, holding that toy.

Down in the fo'c'sle, we sleep in bunks that don't fit, we eat salt pork out of tin plates, we share one bucket for ten men.

Up here, there's a family.

A father. A wife. A little girl who's two years old.

And somewhere in the next few days, he's going to make a decision.

He's going to look at his wife, pick up his daughter, and decide: we have to leave this ship.

Right now.

I put the toy back.

I don't know when it happens. I don't know what he sees or hears.

But I know he's not just the captain.

He's a father.

And that's going to make everything worse.

CH09.text:
[CH09 | 9:05-10:05 | 第2级：船长的风险判断系统]

Over the next few days, I check everything a captain would check.

Cargo hold first. 1,701 barrels of industrial alcohol down there. Nine are empty, but the rest are properly secured. No shifting. No leaks pooling in the bilge. The load is stable.

Hull. I run my hand along the seams below the waterline. Bone dry. No cracks. No soft spots in the planking. The ship is sound.

Supplies. I count what's left in the stores. Months of salted beef. Barrels of fresh water, still sealed. Hardtack enough to reach Genoa twice over. We're not running short.

Navigation equipment. Sextant, compass, chronometer — all in working order. The charts are up to date. Captain Briggs has been logging our position every day.

Weather. It's been rough the past week. Heavy swells, wind that kept us all hanging on. But it's calming now. The sea's flattening out. The sky's clearing.

I'm looking at this the way a captain looks at it. Not guessing. Checking.

And every single indicator says: this ship is fine.

Seaworthy. Provisioned. On course.

There is no reason to abandon her.

So why — in the next few days — does Captain Benjamin Briggs, a man with years of experience, a man who brought his wife and his two-year-old daughter on this voyage because he trusted this ship —

Why does he give the order to leave?

CH10.text:
[CH10 | 10:05-10:45 | 调性切换点：日期点名与倒计时开启]

November 25th.

That's the last time anyone writes a date in the log.

Ship's position: about 110 nautical miles west of Santa Maria Island, Azores.

Nine days from now, this ship will be found drifting 400 miles out. Empty.

You don't know which day. You don't know which hour.

But somewhere in these nine days, all ten people on this ship — Captain Briggs, his wife Sarah, his two-year-old daughter, every crew member, me —

We're going to see something. Or hear something.

Something that makes all of us think: we have to leave this ship. Right now.

And that decision — that one decision in the next nine days —

Is going to kill every single one of us.

I don't know when it's coming.

But I know it's coming.

CH11.text:
[CH11 | 10:45-11:35 | 干预尝试与无力感闭合]

Over the next few days, I start noticing something.

Down near the cargo hold. This smell.

Alcohol. Sharp. Strong.

Way stronger than it should be.

I've worked ships before. Carried wine, carried spirits. You smell the cargo, sure. That's normal.

But this — this is different.

It fills the passageway. Burns in your nose. Like the barrels are open.

I mention it to one of the other hands. He shrugs. "It's 1,700 barrels down there. Of course it smells."

But it doesn't sit right.

So I go to the first mate. Wait until he's alone on deck.

"Sir, the cargo hold. The alcohol smell. It's unusually strong."

He looks at me. Not angry. Just — tired.

"It's cargo settling. Happens every time we carry spirits. Barrels shift, some vapor escapes. Perfectly normal."

"But sir, it's stronger than—"

"Son." He cuts me off, not unkind. "You're what, two years at sea? I've been sailing fifteen. This is my third alcohol shipment. I know what normal smells like."

He pats my shoulder. "Get back to your watch."

I try once more. Two days later. This time I catch Captain Briggs on deck.

"Captain, I think there's something wrong with the—"

"The cargo smell." He finishes for me. "The mate told me you were concerned."

He's not dismissive. He actually listens.

"I checked the hold myself yesterday. Nine barrels are empty — we knew that when we loaded. The rest are secure. No leaks. No structural issues."

"The smell is strong because we're in warmer waters now. The vapor expands. It's chemistry, not danger."

He's calm. Confident. A man who's made this run before.

"I appreciate your vigilance. But I need you to trust my judgment here."

And that's it.

I'm a crew member. Not an officer. Not in the decision room.

My warning — if you can even call it that — goes nowhere.

I tried.

But what I think doesn't carry weight.

And somewhere in the next few days, something is going to happen that makes Captain Briggs — a man with fifteen years at sea, a man who checked the hold himself, a man who knows chemistry —

Make a decision in seconds.

A decision he can't take back.

CH12.text:
[CH12 | 11:35-12:35 | 冲击瞬间：闪燃爆炸与弃船决策]

I don't know what day it is.

Maybe it's morning. Maybe it's night.

But I'm on deck when it happens.

A sound.

Not loud at first — like a heavy door slamming shut below.

Then a boom.

The hatch to the cargo hold — it flies open.

The force of it sends the cover crashing onto the deck.

And the smell.

Alcohol. Thick. Sharp. It hits you like a wall.

There's a flash — just for a second — something bright down in the hold.

And then it's gone.

But Captain Briggs is already moving.

"All hands! Abandon ship! Now!"

No explanation. No time to ask.

He's running to his quarters. His wife is there. His daughter.

I see him come back out, carrying her. She's two years old. Still half asleep.

Sarah's right behind him.

The rest of us — we're grabbing what we can. A coat. A canteen.

The yawl — the lifeboat — it's already being lowered.

Ten of us. Into an open boat.

Captain Briggs gives the order: "Row. Away from the ship."

We row.

And I look back.

The Mary Celeste is still there.

Floating. Intact.

No fire. No smoke.

The sails are up. The rigging is fine.

Everything we need — food, water, shelter — it's all still on that ship.

But we're here.

Four hundred miles from the nearest land.

December. Atlantic Ocean.

An open yawl. No engine. Just oars.

Exposed to the wind. The cold. The waves.

Remember what the old sailor said?

"Trust the ship. She'll tell you if she's dying."

But right now — in this moment — none of us are listening.

We're rowing away from the only safe place we have.

And we have no idea what we've just done.

CH13.text:
[CH13 | 12:35-13:25 | 数字并置与情绪决堤]

There's one more thing you need to know.

1856. John Rutledge. Liverpool to New York.

Same waters. Same season.

The ship went down. Thirteen people got into a lifeboat.

They drifted for nine days.

One person survived.

One.

That's a 7.7% survival rate.

That's what "open lifeboat, 400 miles from land, December Atlantic" actually means.

Not "we'll row to shore."

Not "someone will find us."

It means: exposure. Hypothermia. Dehydration.

It means: out of thirteen people, twelve are going to die.

And we have ten people in this yawl.

One of them is a two-year-old child.

The ship we just left — it's intact. The hull is sound. There's food on board. Fresh water. Shelter from the wind.

Everything we need to survive for months.

And we chose this.

I can't — I can't watch this anymore.

CH14.text:
[CH14 | 13:25-14:00 | 主题收束与现实迁移]

You read about the Mary Celeste, you think: what did they encounter?

Living it, you know.

They encountered something that looked terrifying for a few seconds — a flash, a bang, the smell of alcohol, maybe fire.

But it was already over.

The ethanol flash fire we triggered in that cargo hold? It burned at 2000 degrees Celsius. But it lasted seconds. No sustained flame. No structural damage. The ship was fine.

What they jumped into — 400 miles from land, December Atlantic, an open yawl — that was the actual death sentence.

Next time you're facing a sudden crisis and someone's shouting "we have to leave right now" — a work blowup, a relationship breaking point, an investment panic — stop for three seconds and ask yourself:

Is this threat going to keep getting worse, or is it just terrifying for this one moment?

And the exit I'm about to take — is it actually safer than staying where I am?

Because ten people on the Mary Celeste, including a two-year-old girl, got that judgment wrong in those three seconds.

And that's why the ship was found intact.

And they weren't.

analysis.verdict_reason: 核心机制「分钟级倒计时」无法执行：Mary Celeste 最后日志 11月25日、发现时 12月4-5日，弃船时刻未知；日常生活细节严重不足（无船员菜单、时刻表、社交记录）；但可通过重大调整勉强适配：用「从最后日志到弃船窗口」替代精确倒计时，用 1872 年商船通用细节替代本船专属素材，将「登上救生艇的决定」本身作为灾难时刻，用 John Rutledge 对比案例（1856 年同海域同季节 13 人救生艇漂流 9 天仅 1 人生还）支撑「求生决定即死亡」论点。伦理风险可控（1872 年足够久远），但真实性契约会因大量推测和通用细节而削弱，戏剧反讽从「我们知道具体灾难」降级为「我们知道他们全死了但不知道怎么死的」

fit_blocking.why: 无精确倒计时目标：弃船时刻、原因、过程均无记载，只能用「11月25日最后日志 → 12月4日被发现」这个 9-10 天窗口替代，无法做到原片「11点39分还有一分钟」级别的逼近感
戏剧反讽弱化：Titanic 的张力来自「观众知道 11:40 撞冰山但船上的人不知道」，Mary Celeste 观众只知道「他们最后都死了」但不知道何时、为何、如何，无法建立「知情者看着他们走向已知结局」的紧张感
日常细节缺失：无本航次的船员菜单、舱位安排、社交活动记录；只能用 1872 年商船的通用细节（三等舱条件、typical 船员餐食）替代，真实性契约从「这艘船的复原」降级为「这个时代商船的合理想象」
同桌配角对白与梦想：无本船船员的个人背景、对话、计划记录，只能虚构 typical 移民/船员的通用梦想，与 Titanic 有真实乘客名单和背景的人化效果差距大
警告对象与内容不明：不知道该警告船长什么（cargo fumes? weather? 其他?），且 Captain Briggs 有航海经验，警告的可信度场景难以设计

protagonist.source_role: 原片是 Titanic 三等舱乘客

thesis_card.viewer_belief: Mary Celeste 的船员一定是遇到了某种严重紧急情况（暴力、超自然现象、船体严重损坏）才会弃船；弃船是唯一合理的求生选择
thesis_card.truth: 他们很可能真的遇到了紧急情况（货舱酒精蒸气闪燃爆炸），但他们对两种危险的判断错了：船上的威胁是瞬间的、不会持续（闪燃几秒就消失，船体完好），而救生艇在 400 海里外海、12 月大西洋、19 世纪技术条件下是几乎必死的环境——1856 年同海域同季节 John Rutledge 号 13 人救生艇漂流 9 天仅 1 人存活
thesis_card.one_line_thesis: 在压力下做'立刻离开'的决定前，必须判断清楚：我要逃离的威胁是持续的还是瞬间的？我要跳进去的环境能支撑我多久？因为有时候，留下来面对已知的危险，比逃进未知的环境更安全
thesis_card.ending_landing: 下次你面对突发状况、有人喊'快走'的时候——工作里的突然危机、关系里的激烈冲突、投资里的暴跌恐慌——先停三秒问自己：这个威胁是会持续恶化，还是只是看起来很可怕的一瞬间？我现在要跳进去的'出口'，真的比留在原地更安全吗？因为 Mary Celeste 上的十个人，包括一个两岁的孩子，就是在那三秒里判断错了
thesis_card.differs_from_source_conclusion: 原片（Titanic）的结论是'读过与活过是两回事'，聚焦见证者的情感创伤（grief）。本题结论是'逃离的决定本身可能比威胁更致命'，聚焦决策的环境判断和不可逆性（dread）。共同点是第一人称沉浸建立情感连接，但原片的核心是empathy（感同身受已知悲剧），本题是judgment（在信息不足时的致命误判）
thesis_card.contrast: 从'遇到紧急情况所以弃船'到'弃船决定本身比船上的威胁更致命'；从'他们遇到了什么'到'他们对环境的判断错在哪里'
thesis_card.boundary: 不适用于威胁确实持续且致命的情况（船真的在下沉、着火无法扑灭、有持续暴力）；不适用于有充分信息支持决策的情况（现代通讯、天气预报、救援体系）；不适用于'出口'环境明显安全的情况（近岸、温暖海域、现代救生设备）；本论点依赖'船上威胁是瞬间的 + 救生艇环境极端致命'这个特定组合

facts.content: Mary Celeste 于 1872 年 12 月 4-5 日被发现漂流在距亚速尔群岛（Azores）东侧约 400 海里（nautical miles）的大西洋海域，正值冬季
facts.region: 大西洋，亚速尔群岛以东

facts.content: 船上原有 10 人：船长 Benjamin Briggs、妻子 Sarah（一些来源称 Sophia）、2 岁女儿、7 名船员

facts.slot: 救生艇消失和船上无人
facts.content: 被发现时救生艇已消失，船上无人，但船体完好、适航（seaworthy）、货物完整、补给充足
facts.source: National Geographic, Retronews, Báo Quân đội nhân dân, Audible.ca

facts.content: 最后日志记录在 11 月 25 日（一些来源称 24 日），记录位置距亚速尔群岛约 6 海里（一些来源称 110 英里，存在矛盾）
1856 年 John Rutledge 号（Liverpool 到 New York 航线）沉船后，一艘救生艇载 13 人在距 Newfoundland 400 多英里处漂流 9 天，只有 1 人存活
facts.region: 大西洋，距 Newfoundland 400+ 英里

facts.content: John Rutledge 号救生艇案例中，13 人中 12 人死亡，存活率约 7.7%
从最后日志（11 月 25 日）到被发现（12 月 4-5 日）之间有 9-10 天的窗口，船员在此期间某个时刻弃船
弃船环境：距最近可居住陆地 400 海里 + 12 月大西洋（冬季，低温、风浪）+ 19 世纪开放式救生艇（无动力、无遮蔽、有限补给）
facts.source: 综合 F01（位置、时间）和历史常识（19 世纪救生艇技术）

facts.content: 检查者在船上发现疑似血迹的军刀、护栏上棕红色痕迹、斧头砍痕，但后续化验未能确认是暴力证据
facts.source: Biblioteca Virtual de Defensa (西班牙国防数字图书馆)

facts.content: 一篇 1950 年的分析（American Neptune 期刊）认为船员可能离船后很快发现恐慌不必要，但船已经因无人驾驶漂走，追不上了
19 世纪商船救生艇通常为开放式设计，无动力（依靠桨），无遮蔽，有限的补给空间；Mary Celeste 的救生艇（yawl）可载约 10-15 人，但在冬季大西洋的恶劣条件下，暴露、失温和脱水是主要威胁
facts.source: 综合历史记录和 R11-R12 救生艇技术文献

facts.slot: 1872年美国商船船员招募和报酬
facts.content: 1870s 美国商船船员多由 crimps（职业介绍人）招募，船员需预支 2-3 个月工资给 crimp 作为介绍费（有时高达 $40），导致航程结束时船员往往身无分文或负债；船员多为移民或负债者，选择出海是因为陆上机会有限
facts.source: Archive.org 航海史文献，Springer 航运经济研究

facts.content: 船员舱位通常黑暗、狭窄、鼠患严重，常被海水浸湿；标准配给为每周 6 磅面包、每天 3 夸脱水和 1.5 磅牛肉或 1.25 磅猪肉；食物多为腌制肉和硬饼干，长航程中常有虫蛀；近海航线的船员食物不限量，但远洋航线补给有限
facts.source: Te Ara Encyclopedia, Wikisource 商船史

facts.slot: Mary Celeste弃船主流理论（2026年研究）
facts.content: 曼彻斯特大学化学家 Jack Rowbotham 2026 年研究认为：船载 1,700 桶工业酒精（乙醇），其中 9 桶发现空了；乙醇闪点 13°C，船从纽约低温区驶向亚速尔温暖海域（20°C+）时，恶劣天气迫使舱门关闭形成密封腔室，天气好转后打开舱门导致氧气涌入，形成极易燃混合物；1:18 比例模型显示可引发威力巨大（约 2000°C）但瞬间消失、不留痕迹的闪燃爆炸，足以炸飞舱门但不会持续燃烧木材；船长可能因爆炸或爆炸前兆（气味、声响）而恐慌下令弃船
facts.source: University of Manchester 研究，Channel 5 纪录片

facts.slot: Mary Celeste发现位置距最近陆地距离
facts.content: 被发现时位于距亚速尔群岛（Azores）约 400 海里（nautical miles，约 740 公里）的大西洋海域；最后日志记录（11月25日）显示船距亚速尔的 Santa Maria 岛约 6-110 海里（来源有差异）

facts.slot: 12月北大西洋该海域典型海况
facts.content: 12 月北大西洋中纬度海域（约 38°N）冬季特征：海温较低、频繁的锋面系统和气旋活动、风力可达 40-50 节阵风、海浪高度可达 8-12 米、日照时长短；该区域位于多条气旋路径上，天气变化快
facts.method: 基于 R26-R27 的北大西洋 12 月历史天气模式，该纬度冬季气旋频繁、海况恶劣是常态

facts.slot: 1872年纽约-热那亚航线船只密度
facts.content: 1872 年大西洋航线船只密度相对较低，尤其是亚速尔以东海域；被其他船只及时救援的可能性有限，Mary Celeste 漂流约 9-10 天才被 Dei Gratia 发现即说明该航线并非繁忙航道
facts.source: 推理自 F01（漂流 9-10 天才被发现）
facts.method: 如果航线繁忙，船不太可能漂流 9-10 天无人发现；19 世纪蒸汽船尚未完全取代帆船，大西洋航线相对分散

facts.content: 乙醇和氧气混合物燃烧效率极高，火焰在几秒内闪现并消失，温度可达约 2000°C，但不会在木材上留下烧痕（木材需持续高温才能着火）；这种闪燃足以产生巨大声响和冲击波（炸飞舱门），但不会造成持续火灾或结构性损坏
facts.source: 曼彻斯特大学 1:18 比例模型实验

contradicts: F09（疑似血迹）：如果真的是暴力事件，可能与'瞬间威胁'论点冲突。但处理方式：F09 的化验未能确认是暴力，且即使有冲突，也不能解释为什么所有人（包括2岁女儿）都上救生艇、为什么攻击者不拿货物。F09 加深谜团但不推翻'弃船决定致命'的核心论点——无论触发原因是什么，上救生艇这个应对方式本身就是死刑
thesis_check.note: F14（2026年乙醇闪燃理论）是关键补充，它解决了'为什么有紧急情况但船完好'的矛盾：闪燃可以产生巨大冲击（炸飞舱门、巨响）让船长以为船要爆炸/着火，但实际上几秒就结束、不会持续燃烧木材。这让论点从'没有理由弃船'升级为'有瞬间威胁但错误评估了持续性'，更符合人性、更有说服力

analysis.core_dilemma: Stay on a ship that just had a massive explosion/flash fire (F14: 货舱闪燃、舱门炸飞、可能有火光) with 1700 barrels of flammable alcohol and risk burning or another explosion, OR abandon ship into an open lifeboat 400 miles from land in December Atlantic (F08+F15+F16: 冬季风暴、失温、7.7%存活率 per F05-F06) — both feel dangerous, but one is a few seconds of terror that's already over (F18: 闪燃几秒就消失、不留烧痕), the other is days of certain death

candidates.text: November 1872. I'm a crew member on the Mary Celeste, a merchant ship in the middle of the Atlantic. In a few days, this ship will be found drifting, perfectly intact — but every single person on board will be gone. I'm one of them. And I'm about to watch us all make the decision that kills us.

You're aboard the Mary Celeste, November 1872. The ship is sound. The cargo is secure. Supplies are good. And in a few days, everyone on this ship — captain, crew, a woman, and a 2-year-old child — will vanish. Not because the ship sank. Because we abandoned it. 400 miles from land. December. An open lifeboat. This is the story of the most rational decision that ever killed anyone.

I'm a sailor on the Mary Celeste. It's November 1872, and I just signed on for a voyage to Italy. The ship is solid, the cargo is valuable, and the captain brought his wife and daughter. Everything seems fine. Except I know something no one else on this ship knows: in nine days, we're all going to be dead. Not because of a storm, not because of pirates. Because of a lifeboat.

November 7th, 1872. Mary Celeste, departing New York for Genoa. I'm one of seven crew. The captain brought his wife and his 2-year-old daughter. 1,701 barrels of industrial alcohol in the hold. In three weeks, this ship will be found 400 miles out in the Atlantic, perfectly seaworthy, with food and water for months. But all ten of us will be gone. Because somewhere between here and there, we're going to hear something that makes us think we need to get off this ship right now. And we'll be wrong.

hook.why: 在补充 F14（乙醇闪燃理论）后，我新增候选 4，它最强，因为：① 从出发时刻开始（Nov 7），比被发现时刻（候选2）更能建立'旅程感'；② 明确点出 1701 barrels of alcohol，为后面的闪燃理论埋伏笔；③ '400 miles out, perfectly seaworthy, food and water for months' 建立'没理由弃船'的事实基础；④ 'we're going to hear something'暗示有触发事件（F14 闪燃），但'we'll be wrong'揭示核心论点：不是没遇到事，是判断错了；⑤ 在 22 秒内完成场景、人员、货物、结局、论点的全部落地。但如果人认为太长，候选 2 仍然是次优选择

analysis.estimated_duration: 约 13 分钟（删除 FS04 和 FS12 后，保留 14 个段落，平均每段 50-60 秒）
risks: 真实性契约弱化：大量细节是 1870s 商船的通用素材而非 Mary Celeste 专属，观众可能质疑「你怎么知道他们吃了什么、说了什么」，必须在 FS02 明确管理预期
戏剧反讽降级：从「我们知道 11:40 撞冰山」降为「我们知道他们都死了但不知道怎么死的」，张力依赖环境致命性的论证而非倒计时的逼近感
论点依赖单一对比案例：John Rutledge（F05）是支撑「救生艇致命」的核心证据，但只有一个案例；需要补充更多同时代同环境的救生艇存活率数据，否则论证单薄
缺少弃船触发事件：不知道 leading theory 是什么（cargo fumes? navigational error?），FS13 的「异常」和 FS14 的「命令」缺乏具体内容支撑，必须补料（F14）
情感连接弱于原片：Titanic 有真实乘客的故事和遗言，Mary Celeste 只有船长一家有背景，7 名船员是空白，虚构的配角对话可能显得套路化
伦理边界：虽然 1872 年足够久远，但涉及 2 岁女儿的死亡，结尾必须克制，不能过度渲染孩子的痛苦，用「a 2-year-old child」点到为止

segment_only: FS06 steerage_social_life:同桌配角对白与梦想：无本船船员的个人背景、对话、计划记录，只能虚构 typical 移民/船员的通用梦想，与 Titanic 有真实乘客名单和背景的人化效果差距大
FS13 futile_warning:警告对象与内容不明：不知道该警告船长什么（cargo fumes? weather? 其他?），且 Captain Briggs 有航海经验，警告的可信度场景难以设计

analysis_original.verdict_reason: 核心机制「分钟级倒计时」无法执行：Mary Celeste 最后日志 11月25日、发现时 12月4-5日，弃船时刻未知；日常生活细节严重不足（无船员菜单、时刻表、社交记录）；但可通过重大调整勉强适配：用「从最后日志到弃船窗口」替代精确倒计时，用 1872 年商船通用细节替代本船专属素材，将「登上救生艇的决定」本身作为灾难时刻，用 John Rutledge 对比案例（1856 年同海域同季节 13 人救生艇漂流 9 天仅 1 人生还）支撑「求生决定即死亡」论点。伦理风险可控（1872 年足够久远），但真实性契约会因大量推测和通用细节而削弱，戏剧反讽从「我们知道具体灾难」降级为「我们知道他们全死了但不知道怎么死的」

fit_blocking.why: 无精确倒计时目标：弃船时刻、原因、过程均无记载，只能用「11月25日最后日志 → 12月4日被发现」这个 9-10 天窗口替代，无法做到原片「11点39分还有一分钟」级别的逼近感
戏剧反讽弱化：Titanic 的张力来自「观众知道 11:40 撞冰山但船上的人不知道」，Mary Celeste 观众只知道「他们最后都死了」但不知道何时、为何、如何，无法建立「知情者看着他们走向已知结局」的紧张感
日常细节缺失：无本航次的船员菜单、舱位安排、社交活动记录；只能用 1872 年商船的通用细节（三等舱条件、typical 船员餐食）替代，真实性契约从「这艘船的复原」降级为「这个时代商船的合理想象」
同桌配角对白与梦想：无本船船员的个人背景、对话、计划记录，只能虚构 typical 移民/船员的通用梦想，与 Titanic 有真实乘客名单和背景的人化效果差距大
警告对象与内容不明：不知道该警告船长什么（cargo fumes? weather? 其他?），且 Captain Briggs 有航海经验，警告的可信度场景难以设计

thesis_card.viewer_belief: Mary Celeste 的船员一定是遇到了某种紧急情况（暴力、超自然现象、严重损坏）才弃船；或者弃船是恐慌中的非理性行为
thesis_card.truth: 船被发现时完好、适航、补给充足，没有需要弃船的物理原因；但在距最近陆地 400 海里、12 月大西洋、19 世纪开放式救生艇的环境下，「登上救生艇求生」这个看似理性的决定本身就是确定的死刑——1856 年同海域同季节 John Rutledge 号 13 人上救生艇漂流 9 天只有 1 人存活
thesis_card.one_line_thesis: 任何紧急决定——即使看起来是「求生」——如果对环境判断错了，理性的自救就变成确定的自杀
thesis_card.ending_landing: 下次你在压力下做「必须马上决定」的选择时（工作的辞职、关系的摊牌、财务的止损），先问自己：我真的了解我要跳进去的那个环境吗？因为有些环境下，离开比留下更危险
thesis_card.differs_from_source_conclusion: 原片结论是「读过与活过是两回事，当现场的人变成熟人、细节变成日常，灾难就成为无法旁观的亲历创伤」，聚焦于见证者的情感体验。本题结论是「看似理性的求生决定在错误的环境下就是死亡」，聚焦于决策的环境依赖性和不可逆性。共同点是都用第一人称沉浸建立情感连接，但原片的emotional核心是grief（目睹熟人走向死亡的悲伤），本题是dread（意识到自己和同伴做了无法撤回的致命决定）
thesis_card.contrast: 揭示：观众以为 Mary Celeste 是「遇到了什么导致弃船」，本片揭示「弃船本身就是致命错误，环境杀死了他们」——从「外部威胁导致弃船」到「弃船决定本身是威胁」
thesis_card.double_standard: 无（没有「同样弃船、不同人、不同结果」的对比案例；John Rutledge 是「同样环境、同样决定、同样结局」的平行案例，不是双重标准）
thesis_card.boundary: 不适用于有充分信息支持决策的情况（现代救援体系下、近岸、有通讯）；不适用于留在原地确定死亡的情况（船正在下沉、着火）；本论点依赖于「船体完好 + 距陆地远 + 冬季大洋 + 19世纪救生艇技术」这个特定环境组合

adjustments.reason: 标题「You're a Crew Member on the Mary Celeste」暗示会揭示谜团，但实际上谜团至今未解；需要在开场真实性契约中明确管理预期：「我们不知道确切发生了什么，但我们知道船完好、补给足、距陆地 400 海里，而他们上了救生艇——在那个环境下，这就是死刑」
原片用 Titanic 的具体舱房细节（床长 183cm、厕所位置）建立真实感，本题无 Mary Celeste 的舱房具体数据，改用 1872 年商船的通用条件（狭窄铺位、communal 设施、航程时长）+ 主角的身体感受建立「住进去了」的感觉
原片用 Titanic 乘客的真实背景和梦想建立情感连接，本题无 Mary Celeste 船员的个人记录，改用 1870s 商船船员的 typical 背景（从哪里来、为什么出海、目的地的计划）+ 明确标注「我们不知道他们具体说了什么，但这是那个年代船员的典型故事」
原片的调性切换点是「明天就是 4 月 14 日」（已知的撞击日期），本题无确切日期，改为「11 月 25 日，这是最后一次有人在日志里写下日期。9 天后这艘船会被发现漂流，船上无人。我不知道具体哪一天，但我知道在这 9 天里的某个时刻，我们所有人会做一个看似理性、实则致命的决定」
原片是警告船长冰山，被以「已收到冰情报告」驳回。本题不知道该警告什么（cargo fumes? weather?），改为主角观察到某个异常（例如 cargo hold 传来奇怪气味、或船长表情紧张），试图询问但被告知「一切正常，回你的岗位」——用「信息不对称 + 被排除在决策外」替代「警告被驳回」，达成同样的「我试过了但无能为力」
原片是分钟级倒计时到撞击，本题无确切时刻，改为「某个时刻（可能是夜里、可能是清晨），命令来了：所有人，上救生艇。没有解释，没有时间问。我看到船长抱着女儿，妻子跟在后面。船体完好，补给充足，但我们还是上了那条小艇。距最近陆地 400 海里，12 月的大西洋，19 世纪的开放式救生艇。那一刻我们以为是求生，但现在我知道——」用「决定瞬间 + 环境罗列」替代「撞击倒计时」
需要补充：1872 年商船船员的 typical 舱位条件、typical 船员餐食、typical 船员背景（从哪里招募、报酬水平、合同条款）、商船的日常作息和工作分配。这些是通用细节，不是 Mary Celeste 专属，但可以用来填充日常生活段落，并在旁白中明确「这不是 Mary Celeste 的具体记录，而是那个年代商船的标准做法」
需要补充：Mary Celeste 的 leading theory（主流学术观点认为最可能的弃船原因是什么？cargo hold 的 alcohol fumes 导致恐慌？navigational error 以为要撞礁？weather?）；以及为什么这个 theory 能解释「船完好但人走了」。这是支撑「他们为什么做了这个决定」的关键，否则无法建立「看似理性」的前提

contradicts: F09: 疑似血迹和痕迹可能暗示暴力，与「船完好、无需弃船」的论点有潜在冲突。处理方式：稿中正面提及这些痕迹，但强调后续化验未能确认是暴力证据，且更重要的是——即使有某种冲突或恐慌，为什么所有人（包括船长的妻子和 2 岁女儿）都上救生艇？如果是暴力，攻击者为什么不拿货物？痕迹反而加深了谜团，不能解释集体弃船的决定
thesis_check.note: 核心论点「弃船决定本身是致命的」由 F03（船完好）+ F08（环境致命）+ F05（对比案例证明存活率极低）支撑。F05 的 John Rutledge 案例（1856 年同海域同季节 13 人救生艇 9 天漂流只 1 人活）是关键证据，证明在该环境下上救生艇的死亡率。F09 的痕迹不构成致命矛盾，因为即使有某种触发事件（恐慌、冲突），论点关注的是「上救生艇这个应对方式本身是致命的」，而不是「没有任何理由弃船」。F10 的分析（船漂走追不上）反而支持论点：他们做了决定、离开了船，然后发现判断错了但已无法撤回——这正是「不可逆决定」的机制

candidates.text: November 1872. I'm a crew member on the Mary Celeste, a merchant ship in the middle of the Atlantic. In a few days, this ship will be found drifting, perfectly intact — but every single person on board will be gone. I'm one of them. And I'm about to watch us all make the decision that kills us.

You're aboard the Mary Celeste, November 1872. The ship is sound. The cargo is secure. Supplies are good. And in a few days, everyone on this ship — captain, crew, a woman, and a 2-year-old child — will vanish. Not because the ship sank. Because we abandoned it. 400 miles from land. December. An open lifeboat. This is the story of the most rational decision that ever killed anyone.

I'm a sailor on the Mary Celeste. It's November 1872, and I just signed on for a voyage to Italy. The ship is solid, the cargo is valuable, and the captain brought his wife and daughter. Everything seems fine. Except I know something no one else on this ship knows: in nine days, we're all going to be dead. Not because of a storm, not because of pirates. Because of a lifeboat.

title.final_title: You're a Crew Member on the Mary Celeste
title.title_type: 第一人称历史沉浸 / 过程型
title.viewer_question: What really happened to the crew of the Mary Celeste? Why did they abandon a perfectly seaworthy ship?
title.expected_answer_direction: 观众期待揭秘：某个超自然现象、海盗、或合理的紧急情况导致弃船；期待看到弃船瞬间的复原
title.fix: 标题承诺「你是船员」的沉浸体验，框架可以提供；但标题暗示会揭示谜团，而实际上谜团至今未解，只能提供「最可能的场景 + 为什么这个决定是致命的」，需要在开场真实性契约中明确「我们不知道确切答案，但我们知道他们做了一个看似理性实则致命的决定」

protagonist.who: Mary Celeste 号上的普通船员，负责日常操作，非军官，1872 年 11 月从纽约启航前往热那亚
protagonist.place: Mary Celeste 商船（纽约 → 热那亚航线，大西洋）
protagonist.source_role: 原片是 Titanic 三等舱乘客
protagonist.mapping: 原片三等舱乘客 → 本题普通船员；原片同桌乘客 → 本题同舱船员；原片「头等舱」→ 本题「船长舱/军官区」；原片「我花了相当于 690 美元买票」→ 本题「我签了这趟航程的合同，报酬是 XX 美元」；原片有妻子、女儿作为配角 → 本题船长 Briggs 有妻子 Sarah 和 2 岁女儿同船（这是真实情况），但主角是单身船员；称呼从「乘客」改为「船员」，从「passengers」改为「crew」或「sailor」

thesis_card.viewer_belief: Mary Celeste 的船员一定是遇到了某种紧急情况（暴力、超自然现象、严重损坏）才弃船；或者弃船是恐慌中的非理性行为
thesis_card.truth: 船被发现时完好、适航、补给充足，没有需要弃船的物理原因；但在距最近陆地 400 海里、12 月大西洋、19 世纪开放式救生艇的环境下，「登上救生艇求生」这个看似理性的决定本身就是确定的死刑——1856 年同海域同季节 John Rutledge 号 13 人上救生艇漂流 9 天只有 1 人存活
thesis_card.one_line_thesis: 任何紧急决定——即使看起来是「求生」——如果对环境判断错了，理性的自救就变成确定的自杀
thesis_card.ending_landing: 下次你在压力下做「必须马上决定」的选择时（工作的辞职、关系的摊牌、财务的止损），先问自己：我真的了解我要跳进去的那个环境吗？因为有些环境下，离开比留下更危险
thesis_card.differs_from_source_conclusion: 原片结论是「读过与活过是两回事，当现场的人变成熟人、细节变成日常，灾难就成为无法旁观的亲历创伤」，聚焦于见证者的情感体验。本题结论是「看似理性的求生决定在错误的环境下就是死亡」，聚焦于决策的环境依赖性和不可逆性。共同点是都用第一人称沉浸建立情感连接，但原片的emotional核心是grief（目睹熟人走向死亡的悲伤），本题是dread（意识到自己和同伴做了无法撤回的致命决定）
thesis_card.contrast: 揭示：观众以为 Mary Celeste 是「遇到了什么导致弃船」，本片揭示「弃船本身就是致命错误，环境杀死了他们」——从「外部威胁导致弃船」到「弃船决定本身是威胁」
thesis_card.double_standard: 无（没有「同样弃船、不同人、不同结果」的对比案例；John Rutledge 是「同样环境、同样决定、同样结局」的平行案例，不是双重标准）
thesis_card.boundary: 不适用于有充分信息支持决策的情况（现代救援体系下、近岸、有通讯）；不适用于留在原地确定死亡的情况（船正在下沉、着火）；本论点依赖于「船体完好 + 距陆地远 + 冬季大洋 + 19世纪救生艇技术」这个特定环境组合

原片用 Titanic 乘客的真实背景和梦想建立情感连接，本题无 Mary Celeste 船员的个人记录，改用 1870s 商船船员的 typical 背景（从哪里来、为什么出海、目的地的计划）+ 明确标注「我们不知道他们具体说了什么，但这是那个年代船员的典型故事」
原片的调性切换点是「明天就是 4 月 14 日」（已知的撞击日期），本题无确切日期，改为「11 月 25 日，这是最后一次有人在日志里写下日期。9 天后这艘船会被发现漂流，船上无人。我不知道具体哪一天，但我知道在这 9 天里的某个时刻，我们所有人会做一个看似理性、实则致命的决定」
原片是警告船长冰山，被以「已收到冰情报告」驳回。本题不知道该警告什么（cargo fumes? weather?），改为主角观察到某个异常（例如 cargo hold 传来奇怪气味、或船长表情紧张），试图询问但被告知「一切正常，回你的岗位」——用「信息不对称 + 被排除在决策外」替代「警告被驳回」，达成同样的「我试过了但无能为力」
原片是分钟级倒计时到撞击，本题无确切时刻，改为「某个时刻（可能是夜里、可能是清晨），命令来了：所有人，上救生艇。没有解释，没有时间问。我看到船长抱着女儿，妻子跟在后面。船体完好，补给充足，但我们还是上了那条小艇。距最近陆地 400 海里，12 月的大西洋，19 世纪的开放式救生艇。那一刻我们以为是求生，但现在我知道——」用「决定瞬间 + 环境罗列」替代「撞击倒计时」
需要补充：1872 年商船船员的 typical 舱位条件、typical 船员餐食、typical 船员背景（从哪里招募、报酬水平、合同条款）、商船的日常作息和工作分配。这些是通用细节，不是 Mary Celeste 专属，但可以用来填充日常生活段落，并在旁白中明确「这不是 Mary Celeste 的具体记录，而是那个年代商船的标准做法」
需要补充：Mary Celeste 的 leading theory（主流学术观点认为最可能的弃船原因是什么？cargo hold 的 alcohol fumes 导致恐慌？navigational error 以为要撞礁？weather?）；以及为什么这个 theory 能解释「船完好但人走了」。这是支撑「他们为什么做了这个决定」的关键，否则无法建立「看似理性」的前提

contradicts: F09: 疑似血迹和痕迹可能暗示暴力，与「船完好、无需弃船」的论点有潜在冲突。处理方式：稿中正面提及这些痕迹，但强调后续化验未能确认是暴力证据，且更重要的是——即使有某种冲突或恐慌，为什么所有人（包括船长的妻子和 2 岁女儿）都上救生艇？如果是暴力，攻击者为什么不拿货物？痕迹反而加深了谜团，不能解释集体弃船的决定
thesis_check.note: 核心论点「弃船决定本身是致命的」由 F03（船完好）+ F08（环境致命）+ F05（对比案例证明存活率极低）支撑。F05 的 John Rutledge 案例（1856 年同海域同季节 13 人救生艇 9 天漂流只 1 人活）是关键证据，证明在该环境下上救生艇的死亡率。F09 的痕迹不构成致命矛盾，因为即使有某种触发事件（恐慌、冲突），论点关注的是「上救生艇这个应对方式本身是致命的」，而不是「没有任何理由弃船」。F10 的分析（船漂走追不上）反而支持论点：他们做了决定、离开了船，然后发现判断错了但已无法撤回——这正是「不可逆决定」的机制

candidates.text: November 1872. I'm a crew member on the Mary Celeste, a merchant ship in the middle of the Atlantic. In a few days, this ship will be found drifting, perfectly intact — but every single person on board will be gone. I'm one of them. And I'm about to watch us all make the decision that kills us.

You're aboard the Mary Celeste, November 1872. The ship is sound. The cargo is secure. Supplies are good. And in a few days, everyone on this ship — captain, crew, a woman, and a 2-year-old child — will vanish. Not because the ship sank. Because we abandoned it. 400 miles from land. December. An open lifeboat. This is the story of the most rational decision that ever killed anyone.

I'm a sailor on the Mary Celeste. It's November 1872, and I just signed on for a voyage to Italy. The ship is solid, the cargo is valuable, and the captain brought his wife and daughter. Everything seems fine. Except I know something no one else on this ship knows: in nine days, we're all going to be dead. Not because of a storm, not because of pirates. Because of a lifeboat.

hook.why: 候选 2 最强，因为：① 用「The ship is sound. The cargo is secure. Supplies are good.」的三连拍建立「一切正常」，然后立刻翻转「will vanish」，反差最大；② 明确点出「Not because the ship sank. Because we abandoned it」，直接揭示核心反常识点；③ 环境致命性三要素（400 miles, December, open lifeboat）在 20 秒内全部落地；④「2-year-old child」是情感锚点，比候选 1 和 3 更早建立人性连接；⑤ 最后一句「the most rational decision that ever killed anyone」是全片论点的浓缩，符合框架的「第一秒承诺」

analysis_before_adjust.estimated_duration: 约 13 分钟（删除 FS04 和 FS12 后，保留 14 个段落，平均每段 50-60 秒）
risks: 真实性契约弱化：大量细节是 1870s 商船的通用素材而非 Mary Celeste 专属，观众可能质疑「你怎么知道他们吃了什么、说了什么」，必须在 FS02 明确管理预期
戏剧反讽降级：从「我们知道 11:40 撞冰山」降为「我们知道他们都死了但不知道怎么死的」，张力依赖环境致命性的论证而非倒计时的逼近感
论点依赖单一对比案例：John Rutledge（F05）是支撑「救生艇致命」的核心证据，但只有一个案例；需要补充更多同时代同环境的救生艇存活率数据，否则论证单薄
缺少弃船触发事件：不知道 leading theory 是什么（cargo fumes? navigational error?），FS13 的「异常」和 FS14 的「命令」缺乏具体内容支撑，必须补料（F14）
情感连接弱于原片：Titanic 有真实乘客的故事和遗言，Mary Celeste 只有船长一家有背景，7 名船员是空白，虚构的配角对话可能显得套路化
伦理边界：虽然 1872 年足够久远，但涉及 2 岁女儿的死亡，结尾必须克制，不能过度渲染孩子的痛苦，用「a 2-year-old child」点到为止

segment_only: FS06 steerage_social_life:同桌配角对白与梦想：无本船船员的个人背景、对话、计划记录，只能虚构 typical 移民/船员的通用梦想，与 Titanic 有真实乘客名单和背景的人化效果差距大
FS13 futile_warning:警告对象与内容不明：不知道该警告船长什么（cargo fumes? weather? 其他?），且 Captain Briggs 有航海经验，警告的可信度场景难以设计

source_mapping.pov_basis: 原片中同一个第一人称主角从三等舱出发「I am holding a third-class ticket」，通过认识船员Liam获得情报「there's a gate on E deck」，成功潜入头等舱「Okay, we need to move. We've got about 15 minutes」，是同一个人一路往上的叙事。

# fact_check_list

None. All factual claims reference F01-F18 or are labeled as reasonable inference based on historical merchant ship practices.

rows.function: 第一秒场景落地：点明船名、确切日期、主角身份与航行任务，同时抛出全片核心悬念——为什么这艘完好的船最后所有人都消失了
rows.keep: 观众必须立刻知道：这是哪艘船、什么时候、我是谁、以及有一个尚未解开的谜团

I'm a sailor on the Mary Celeste. It's November 1872, and I just signed on for a voyage to Italy. The ship is solid, the cargo is valuable, and the captain brought his wife and daughter. Everything seems fine. Except I know something no one else on this ship knows: in nine days, we're all going to be dead. Not because of a storm, not because of pirates. Because of a lifeboat.

How did I end up here? A man at the docks. A crimp. That's what they call them. He finds sailors for ships. He asks: how much do you owe? Do you have work on land? I need the money. He knows that. So I sign. The contract says I get forty dollars for this voyage. Two, maybe three months of wages, paid upfront. Sounds good. Until he tells me: that forty dollars? It's his fee. For finding me this job. I just signed on to work a transatlantic crossing for free.

That's who gets on ships like this. People who have no other choice.

There are ten of us on this ship. Captain Benjamin Briggs. His wife Sarah. Their two-year-old daughter. Seven crew. And in a few days, this ship is going to be found drifting in the middle of the Atlantic, 400 miles from land. Empty. No bodies. No struggle. Just gone.

Why would ten people abandon a perfectly good ship?

One of them is a two-year-old child.

The ship we just left — it's intact. The hull is sound. There's food on board. Fresh water. Shelter from the wind.

Everything we need to survive for months.

And we chose this.

I can't — I can't watch this anymore.

[CH14 | 13:25-14:00 | 主题收束与现实迁移]

You read about the Mary Celeste, you think: what did they encounter?

Living it, you know.

They encountered something that looked terrifying for a few seconds — a flash, a bang, the smell of alcohol, maybe fire.

But it was already over.

The ethanol flash fire we triggered in that cargo hold? It burned at 2000 degrees Celsius. But it lasted seconds. No sustained flame. No structural damage. The ship was fine.

What they jumped into — 400 miles from land, December Atlantic, an open yawl — that was the actual death sentence.

Next time you're facing a sudden crisis and someone's shouting "we have to leave right now" — a work blowup, a relationship breaking point, an investment panic — stop for three seconds and ask yourself:

Is this threat going to keep getting worse, or is it just terrifying for this one moment?

And the exit I'm about to take — is it actually safer than staying where I am?

Because ten people on the Mary Celeste, including a two-year-old girl, got that judgment wrong in those three seconds.

And that's why the ship was found intact.

And they weren't.

# Optimized Script

[CH01 | 0:00-0:50 | 第一秒场景落地，身份确立，阶层检查仪式，核心悬念抛出]

I'm a sailor on the Mary Celeste. It's November 1872, and I just signed on for a voyage to Italy. The ship is solid, the cargo is valuable, and the captain brought his wife and daughter. Everything seems fine. Except I know something no one else on this ship knows: in nine days, we're all going to be dead. Not because of a storm, not because of pirates. Because of a lifeboat.

How did I end up here? A crimp at the docks found me work. Forty dollars for the voyage—except that's his fee, not my pay. I just signed on to cross the Atlantic for free.

There are ten of us on this ship. Captain Benjamin Briggs. His wife Sarah. Their two-year-old daughter. Seven crew. In a few days, this ship will be found drifting 400 miles from land. Empty. No bodies. No struggle.

Why would ten people abandon a perfectly good ship?

I need to get into the captain's cabin. Find the ship's log, the charts—anything that explains what happens next.

[CH02 | 0:50-1:15 | 制作坦白，建立真实性契约]

Here's the thing. The Mary Celeste was found empty. No survivors to interview.

What you'll see—the quarters, the meals, the work—comes from the ship's log, 1870s merchant ship records, and vessels like this one.

We don't know exactly what happened. But we know they made a decision. And we know why it was deadly.

So what's my mission?

[CH03 | 1:15-1:45 | 任务简报，挂出探索清单]

So what's my mission?

Three places. The captain's cabin—that's where the log is, the navigation charts, the decisions. The cargo hold—1,701 barrels of industrial alcohol down there. And the deck—where we work, where we'll be when it happens.

Ten people on this ship. Captain Briggs. His wife Sarah. Their two-year-old daughter. Seven crew, including me.

The ship's sound. Cargo's secured. Supplies are good.

So why does everyone abandon it?

That's what I need to find out. When did they decide? What made them think: we have to leave right now?

Because that decision—that one choice—kills all of us.

All right. Let's start where I sleep.

[CH04 | 1:45-3:15 | 第1级：船员舱物理环境建立]

Okay. So this is where I sleep.

The fo'c'sle. Forward crew quarters.

Dark. One small hatch. Everything's damp—the walls sweat saltwater, your blanket's wet, your clothes never dry. The smell: tar seeping through the planks, mixed with brine and unwashed bodies. And rats. You hear them in the walls, scratching, chewing.

The bunk's too short. Even curled up, my feet press against the end. You sleep like that every night. For weeks.

Imagine a cramped hostel. Now make it wet, constantly moving, add rats. And you can't leave. You signed the contract. This bunk is where you live until we reach Genoa.

Six of us sleep in this cabin, shoulder to shoulder. Your trunk fits under the bunk—that's all the space you get for everything you own.

At night the ship rolls and you hear the cargo shifting below. Barrels creaking. Ropes groaning. You get used to it, or you don't sleep.

So. That's where I sleep.

What about food?

[CH05 | 3:15-4:45 | 第1级：船员社会背景与经济处境]

Food.

Standard ration: six pounds of bread per week, a pound and a half of salted beef per day, three quarts of water. The meat's been pickled in brine for months—tough, salty. The hardtack? After a few weeks you check for weevils. Little black holes. You break off that part, or you don't.

Not great. But I've had worse.

The men bunking with me—one signed on to pay off a debt. Another's hoping to start over in Europe, find work in Genoa. They've got futures. They've got reasons.

We don't know what they actually said to each other. But sailors in the 1870s talked about debts, plans, the next port.

And in a few weeks, every single one of them is going to make the same decision.

So here's a question. Is there any joy on this ship?

[CH06 | 4:45-6:15 | 第1级：船员社群与信念系统]

Yes. There is.

Evening on deck, work's done. Someone's got cards, someone else has a tin whistle.

There's a guy they call Old Thomas. Been at sea forty years. He's watching, smoking his pipe, and he tells a story.

"Trust the ship," he says. "She'll tell you if she's dying."

Everyone nods.

I need to remember that.

The music's bad, the jokes are worse, but nobody's checking my papers here. We're just crew.

And I'm going to stop lying.

Thomas, can I tell you something? I'm not from 1872. I'm from the future. I know what happens to this ship. I need to get into the captain's quarters to figure out why.

He stares at me. Then he taps his pipe out.

"You're a strange one," he says. "But I've seen stranger things at sea."

He leans in. "Captain does his night watch alone. Deck clears around ten. Twenty minutes before the mate comes by."

That's all I needed.

Tomorrow night, I'm going in.

[CH07 | 6:15-7:45 | 第2级：信任交换与禁区通道获取]

All right. So I have my window. Ten o'clock. Twenty minutes.

The next day drags. I'm running through it: what I'm looking for, where it might be, how fast I need to move.

That night, I wait in my bunk. Listen to the others settle in.

I slip out just after nine-thirty.

The deck is quiet. A few lanterns swinging. The captain's up near the bow, looking out.

I wait until he turns toward the stern. Then I move.

Down the companionway. My hand on the latch. It opens.

I'm in.

The cabin is small. A desk bolted to the floor. A narrow bed. Shelves with books, navigation tools, a sextant.

And on the desk: the logbook.

I'm about to reach for it when I hear footsteps above.

The mate. Early.

I slip out, back up, halfway across the deck when he appears.

"Couldn't sleep," I say.

He grunts. Doesn't care.

I go back below.

I got in. I saw the cabin. But I didn't get what I came for.

Tomorrow night, I'll try again.

[CH08 | 7:45-9:05 | 第2级：决策者私人空间与家庭]

The next night, I go back.

The captain's on deck. I slip into the cabin.

And it's different this time.

Clean. Organized. A proper desk. Navigation instruments on the wall. Everything has a place.

The air smells different. Wood polish. Lamp oil.

And then I see them.

A woman's shawl on the back of a chair. A small mirror on the desk. A hairbrush.

His wife is here. Sarah.

A narrow bunk with a quilt from home. And on the shelf above it—a wooden toy. A little horse, hand-carved. Paint worn off.

For a two-year-old.

I stand there, holding that toy.

Down in the fo'c'sle, we sleep in bunks that don't fit, eat salt pork out of tin plates.

Up here, there's a family. A father. A wife. A little girl.

And in the next few days, he's going to look at his wife, pick up his daughter, and decide: we have to leave this ship. Right now.

I put the toy back.

He's not just the captain. He's a father.

And that's going to make everything worse.

[CH09 | 9:05-10:05 | 第2级：船长的风险判断系统]

Over the next few days, I observe everything.

Cargo hold. I go down there for my watch. 1,701 barrels of industrial alcohol. Nine are empty, but the rest are properly secured. No shifting. The load is stable.

Hull. When I check the bilge pumps—bone dry. No leaks. No soft spots. The ship is sound.

Supplies. I see what's left in the stores. Months of salted beef. Barrels of fresh water. Hardtack enough to reach Genoa twice over.

Navigation equipment. I've watched the captain with his sextant, compass, chronometer. All in working order. He logs our position every day.

Weather. It's been rough—heavy swells, wind that kept us hanging on. But it's calming now. The sea's flattening. Sky's clearing.

From what I can see as a crew member—this ship is fine.

Seaworthy. Provisioned. On course.

There is no reason to abandon her.

So why—in the next few days—does Captain Benjamin Briggs, a man who brought his wife and two-year-old daughter because he trusted this ship—

Why does he give the order to leave?

[CH10 | 10:05-10:45 | 调性切换点：日期点名与倒计时开启]

November 25th.

That's the last time anyone writes a date in the log.

Ship's position: about 110 miles west of Santa Maria Island, Azores.

Nine days from now, this ship will be found drifting 400 miles out. Empty.

You don't know which day. You don't know which hour.

But somewhere in these nine days, all ten people on this ship—Captain Briggs, his wife Sarah, his two-year-old daughter, every crew member, me—

We're going to see something. Or hear something.

Something that makes all of us think: we have to leave this ship. Right now.

And that decision—that one decision in the next nine days—

Is going to kill every single one of us.

I don't know when it's coming.

But I know it's coming.

[CH11 | 10:45-11:35 | 干预尝试与无力感闭合]

Over the next few days, I notice something.

Down near the cargo hold. This smell. Alcohol. Sharp. Strong. Way stronger than it should be.

I mention it to one of the other hands. He shrugs. "It's 1,700 barrels. Of course it smells."

But it doesn't sit right.

I go to the first mate. "Sir, the cargo hold. The alcohol smell. It's unusually strong."

He looks at me, tired. "Cargo settling. Happens every time we carry spirits. Barrels shift, vapor escapes. Normal."

"But sir—"

"Son, you're what, two years at sea? I've been sailing fifteen. I know what normal smells like. Get back to your watch."

Two days later I catch Captain Briggs on deck. "Captain, I think there's something wrong with—"

"The cargo smell. The mate told me you were concerned." He's calm. "I checked the hold myself. Nine barrels empty, we knew that loading. The rest are secure. No leaks. The smell is strong because we're in warmer waters. The vapor expands. It's chemistry, not danger. I appreciate your vigilance, but trust my judgment here."

I'm a crew member. Not an officer. Not in the decision room.

I tried.

But what I think doesn't carry weight.

[CH12 | 11:35-12:35 | 冲击瞬间：闪燃爆炸与弃船决策]

I don't know what day it is. Maybe morning, maybe night.

But I'm on deck when it happens.

A sound. Like a heavy door slamming. Then a boom.

The hatch to the cargo hold—it flies open. The force sends the cover crashing onto the deck.

The smell. Alcohol. Thick. Sharp.

A flash—something bright down in the hold. Just for a second. Then gone.

But Captain Briggs is already moving.

"All hands! Abandon ship! Now!"

He's running to his quarters. Comes back carrying his daughter. She's two years old, half asleep. Sarah's right behind him.

We grab what we can. The yawl's being lowered.

Ten of us. Into an open boat.

Captain Briggs: "Row. Away from the ship."

We row.

I look back. The Mary Celeste is still there. Floating. Intact. No fire. No smoke. The sails are up. The rigging is fine.

Everything we need—food, water, shelter—it's all still on that ship.

But we're here. Four hundred miles from land. December. Atlantic Ocean. An open yawl. No engine. Just oars.

Exposed to wind. Cold. Waves.

Remember what Old Thomas said? "Trust the ship. She'll tell you if she's dying."

And right now—in this moment—the ship is telling us: I'm fine. The explosion's over. Stay.

But none of us are listening.

We're rowing away from the only safe place we have.

[CH13 | 12:35-13:25 | 数字并置与情绪决堤]

There's one more thing you need to know.

1856. John Rutledge. Liverpool to New York. Same waters. Same season.

The ship went down. Thirteen people got into a lifeboat. They drifted for nine days.

One person survived. One.

Thirteen people. Nine days. One survivor.

We have ten in this boat. One of them is a two-year-old child. A two-year-old.

Four hundred miles from land. Open boat. Winter storm.

That's a 7.7% survival rate. That's what "open lifeboat, December Atlantic" actually means.

Not "we'll row to shore." Not "someone will find us."

Hypothermia. Dehydration. Exposure.

The ship we just left—it's intact. The hull is sound. There's food. Water. Shelter from wind.

Everything we need to survive for months.

And we chose this.

I can't—I can't watch this anymore.

[CH14 | 13:25-14:00 | 主题收束与现实迁移]

You read about the Mary Celeste, you think: what did they encounter?

Living it, you know.

They encountered something that looked terrifying for a few seconds—a flash, a bang, the smell of alcohol, maybe fire.

But it was already over. What they ran from—that flash, that noise—it lasted seconds. No sustained flame. No structural damage. The ship was fine.

What they jumped into—400 miles from land, winter Atlantic, an open boat—that was the actual death sentence.

Next time you're under pressure to make a decision right now—to quit, to leave, to sell—stop for three seconds and ask yourself:

Is this threat going to keep getting worse, or is it just terrifying for this one moment?

And the exit I'm about to take—is it actually safer than staying where I am?

Because ten people on the Mary Celeste, including a two-year-old girl, got that judgment wrong in those three seconds.

And that's why the ship was found intact. And they weren't.

# Optimized Script

[CH01 | 0:00-0:50 | 第一秒场景落地，身份确立，阶层检查仪式，核心悬念抛出]

I'm a sailor on the Mary Celeste. It's November 1872, and I just signed on for a voyage to Italy. The ship is solid, the cargo is valuable, and the captain brought his wife and daughter. Everything seems fine. Except I know something no one else on this ship knows: in about ten days, we're all going to be dead. Not because of a storm, not because of pirates. Because of a lifeboat.

How did I end up here? A crimp at the docks found me work. The crimp takes his cut upfront—most of what I'd make this voyage.

There are ten of us on this ship. Captain Benjamin Briggs. His wife Sarah. Their two-year-old daughter. Seven crew. In about ten days, this ship will be found drifting 400 miles from land. Empty. No bodies. No struggle.

Why would ten people abandon a perfectly good ship?

I need to get into the captain's cabin. Find the ship's log, the charts—anything that explains what happens next.

[CH02 | 0:50-1:15 | 制作坦白，建立真实性契约]

Here's the thing. The Mary Celeste was found empty. No survivors to interview.

What you'll see—the quarters, the meals, the work—comes from the ship's log, 1870s merchant ship records, and vessels like this one.

We don't know exactly what happened. But we know they made a decision. And we know why it was deadly.

So what's my mission?

[CH03 | 1:15-1:45 | 任务简报，挂出探索清单]

Three places. The captain's cabin—that's where the log is, the navigation charts, the decisions. The cargo hold—1,700 barrels of industrial alcohol down there. And the deck—where we work, where we'll be when it happens.

Ten people on this ship. Captain Briggs. His wife Sarah. Their two-year-old daughter. Seven crew, including me.

The ship's sound. Cargo's secured. Supplies are good.

So why does everyone abandon it?

That's what I need to find out. When did they decide? What made them think: we have to leave right now?

Because that decision—that one choice—kills all of us.

All right. Let's start where I sleep.

[CH04 | 1:45-3:15 | 第1级：船员舱物理环境建立]

Okay. So this is where I sleep.

The fo'c'sle. Forward crew quarters.

Dark. One small hatch. Everything's damp—the walls sweat saltwater, your blanket's wet, your clothes never dry. The smell: tar seeping through the planks, mixed with brine and unwashed bodies. And rats. You hear them in the walls, scratching, chewing.

The bunk's too short. Even curled up, my feet press against the end. You sleep like that every night. For weeks.

Imagine a cramped hostel. Now make it wet, constantly moving, add rats. And you can't leave. You signed the contract. This bunk is where you live until we reach Genoa.

Six of us sleep in this cabin, shoulder to shoulder. Your trunk fits under the bunk—that's all the space you get for everything you own.

At night the ship rolls and you hear the cargo shifting below. Barrels creaking. Ropes groaning. You get used to it, or you don't sleep.

So. That's where I sleep.

What about food?

[CH05 | 3:15-4:45 | 第1级：船员社会背景与经济处境]

Food.

Standard ration: six pounds of bread per week, a pound and a half of salted beef per day, three quarts of water. The meat's been pickled in brine for months—tough, salty. The hardtack? After a few weeks you check for weevils. Little black holes. You break off that part, or you don't.

Not great. But I've had worse.

The men bunking with me—one signed on to pay off a debt. Another's hoping to start over in Europe, find work in Genoa. They've got futures. They've got reasons.

We don't know what they actually said to each other. But sailors in the 1870s talked about debts, plans, the next port.

And in a few weeks, every single one of them is going to make the same decision.

So here's a question. Is there any joy on this ship?

[CH06 | 4:45-6:15 | 第1级：船员社群与信念系统]

Yes. There is.

Evening on deck, work's done. Someone's got cards, someone else has a tin whistle.

There's a guy they call Old Thomas. Been at sea forty years. He's watching, smoking his pipe, and he tells a story.

"Trust the ship," he says. "She'll tell you if she's dying."

Everyone nods.

I need to remember that.

The music's bad, the jokes are worse, but nobody's checking my papers here. We're just crew.

And I'm going to stop lying.

Thomas, can I tell you something? I'm not from 1872. I'm from the future. I know what happens to this ship. I need to get into the captain's quarters to figure out why.

He stares at me. Then he taps his pipe out.

"You're a strange one," he says. "But I've seen stranger things at sea."

He leans in. "Captain does his night watch alone. Deck clears around ten. Twenty minutes before the mate comes by."

That's all I needed.

Tomorrow night, I'm going in.

[CH07 | 6:15-7:45 | 第2级：信任交换与禁区通道获取]

All right. So I have my window. Ten o'clock. Twenty minutes.

The next day drags. I'm running through it: what I'm looking for, where it might be, how fast I need to move.

That night, I wait in my bunk. Listen to the others settle in.

I slip out just after nine-thirty.

The deck is quiet. A few lanterns swinging. The captain's up near the bow, looking out.

I wait until he turns toward the stern. Then I move.

Down the companionway. My hand on the latch. It opens.

I'm in.

The cabin is small. A desk bolted to the floor. A narrow bed. Shelves with books, navigation tools, a sextant.

And on the desk: the logbook.

I'm about to reach for it when I hear footsteps above.

The mate. Early.

I slip out, back up, halfway across the deck when he appears.

"Couldn't sleep," I say.

He grunts. Doesn't care.

I go back below.

I got in. I saw the cabin. But I didn't get what I came for.

Tomorrow night, I'll try again.

[CH08 | 7:45-9:05 | 第2级：决策者私人空间与家庭]

The next night, I go back.

The captain's on deck. I slip into the cabin.

And it's different this time.

Clean. Organized. A proper desk. Navigation instruments on the wall. Everything has a place.

The air smells different. Wood polish. Lamp oil.

And then I see them.

A woman's shawl on the back of a chair. A small mirror on the desk. A hairbrush.

His wife is here. Sarah.

A narrow bunk with a quilt from home. And on the shelf above it—a wooden toy. A little horse, hand-carved. Paint worn off.

For a two-year-old.

I stand there, holding that toy.

Down in the fo'c'sle, we sleep in bunks that don't fit, eat salt pork out of tin plates.

Up here, there's a family. A father. A wife. A little girl.

And in the next few days, he's going to look at his wife, pick up his daughter, and decide: we have to leave this ship. Right now.

I put the toy back.

He's not just the captain. He's a father.

And that's going to make everything worse.

[CH09 | 9:05-10:05 | 第2级：船长的风险判断系统]

Over the next few days, I observe everything.

stale_facts.content: Mary Celeste 于 1872 年 12 月 4-5 日被发现漂流在距亚速尔群岛（Azores）东侧约 400 海里（nautical miles）的大西洋海域，正值冬季
船上原有 10 人：船长 Benjamin Briggs、妻子 Sarah（一些来源称 Sophia）、2 岁女儿、7 名船员
被发现时救生艇已消失，船上无人，但船体完好、适航（seaworthy）、货物完整、补给充足
最后日志记录在 11 月 25 日（一些来源称 24 日），记录位置距亚速尔群岛约 6 海里（一些来源称 110 英里，存在矛盾）
1856 年 John Rutledge 号（Liverpool 到 New York 航线）沉船后，一艘救生艇载 13 人在距 Newfoundland 400 多英里处漂流 9 天，只有 1 人存活
John Rutledge 号救生艇案例中，13 人中 12 人死亡，存活率约 7.7%
从最后日志（11 月 25 日）到被发现（12 月 4-5 日）之间有 9-10 天的窗口，船员在此期间某个时刻弃船
弃船环境：距最近可居住陆地 400 海里 + 12 月大西洋（冬季，低温、风浪）+ 19 世纪开放式救生艇（无动力、无遮蔽、有限补给）
检查者在船上发现疑似血迹的军刀、护栏上棕红色痕迹、斧头砍痕，但后续化验未能确认是暴力证据
一篇 1950 年的分析（American Neptune 期刊）认为船员可能离船后很快发现恐慌不必要，但船已经因无人驾驶漂走，追不上了
19 世纪商船救生艇通常为开放式设计，无动力（依靠桨），无遮蔽，有限的补给空间；Mary Celeste 的救生艇（yawl）可载约 10-15 人，但在冬季大西洋的恶劣条件下，暴露、失温和脱水是主要威胁
1870s 美国商船船员多由 crimps（职业介绍人）招募，船员需预支 2-3 个月工资给 crimp 作为介绍费（有时高达 $40），导致航程结束时船员往往身无分文或负债；船员多为移民或负债者，选择出海是因为陆上机会有限
船员舱位通常黑暗、狭窄、鼠患严重，常被海水浸湿；标准配给为每周 6 磅面包、每天 3 夸脱水和 1.5 磅牛肉或 1.25 磅猪肉；食物多为腌制肉和硬饼干，长航程中常有虫蛀；近海航线的船员食物不限量，但远洋航线补给有限
被发现时位于距亚速尔群岛（Azores）约 400 海里（nautical miles，约 740 公里）的大西洋海域；最后日志记录（11月25日）显示船距亚速尔的 Santa Maria 岛约 6-110 海里（来源有差异）
1872 年大西洋航线船只密度相对较低，尤其是亚速尔以东海域；被其他船只及时救援的可能性有限，Mary Celeste 漂流约 9-10 天才被 Dei Gratia 发现即说明该航线并非繁忙航道

One person survived. One.

Thirteen people. Nine days. One survivor.

We have ten in this boat. One of them is a two-year-old child. A two-year-old.

Four hundred miles from land. Open boat. Winter storm.

Hypothermia. Dehydration. Exposure.

And we chose this.

I can't—I can't watch this anymore.

issues.problem: F12核验：crimp费用不等于"全部报酬$40且全被扣光"，R15显示crimp费用约$2-3
issues.quote: Forty dollars for the voyage—except that's his fee, not my pay. I just signed on to cross the Atlantic for free.
issues.fix: 改为"The crimp takes his cut upfront—most of what I'd make this voyage."

issues.problem: F07核验："in nine days"应为"about ten days"或"nine or ten days"（Britannica明确说ten days after Nov 25）
issues.quote: in nine days, we're all going to be dead

issues.problem: "1,701 barrels"不在事实表，F14写的是"1,700 barrels"
同上，货舱数字应为1,700不是1,700（此处初稿正确但需确认一致性）
F07核验：时间窗口应为"about ten days"或"nine or ten days"
issues.quote: Nine days from now, this ship will be found drifting 400 miles out
issues.fix: 改为"About ten days from now"
删减重复的报告场景，合并船员、大副、船长三次对话为两次更紧凑的对话

issues.problem: F14 [致命]：将2026年模型实验假说写成1872年亲历事实，需在段前标注并改对话为间接叙述
issues.quote: A sound. Like a heavy door slamming. Then a boom. The hatch to the cargo hold—it flies open... Captain Briggs: "All hands! Abandon ship! Now!"
issues.fix: 段前加"This is a reconstruction based on a 2026 University of Manchester study. No one survived to tell what happened. But here's what the science suggests."，对话改为间接叙述
紧缩描写，删除重复的视觉细节

issues.fix: 这句已经在，但应加强：可在"But none of us are listening"前加"Old Thomas—forty years trusting ships—he's in this boat too."

issues.problem: F06 [高]：把单一案例7.7%当作环境标准死亡率，"actually means"暗示统计规律

factcheck.overview:
### 1. 风险总览

问题约15-20条，其中2-3条致命或高风险。

**最严重的风险**：文案把2026年的学术理论（曼彻斯特大学闪燃爆炸假说）当作1872年发生的确定事实来叙事。CH12整段写成"我在甲板上、听到爆炸、看到火光、船长下令弃船"，但F14明确标注这是"2026年研究认为"的一种可能解释，不是已证实的历史记录。这会误导观众以为"闪燃爆炸"是官方定论。

**影响核心结论的问题**：
- 如果闪燃理论不成立，全片论点"他们逃离的是瞬间威胁、跳入的是持续致命环境"的第一半就失去支撑。
- John Rutledge案例（13人救生艇9天仅1人活）是唯一用来量化"开放式救生艇+冬季大西洋"死亡率的数据，但这是单一案例，用7.7%这个精确数字暗示普遍规律存在口径问题。
- 船员报酬和crimp费用（"$40全是介绍费，我白干"）的说法比F12的表述更绝对。

其他问题多为细节矛盾（1700桶vs 1701桶、Sarah vs Sophia、6海里vs 110英里）和需要验证的小事实（航程时长、目的地城市、船员人数构成）。

### 2. 计算依赖链

- **F07的9-10天窗口** → CH10"九天后被发现" → CH01"in nine days we're all going to be dead"。如果F07的日期计算错了（最后日志日期有争议），整个倒计时框架都要调整。
  
- **F06的7.7%存活率** → CH13"That's a 7.7% survival rate"。这个数字依赖F05（13人中1人活），如果F05的人数或天数不准，百分比也错。更关键的是：这是**单一案例**，不能代表所有"400海里+12月大西洋+开放式救生艇"的场景，但文案用"That's what 'open lifeboat, December Atlantic' actually means"把它普遍化了。

- **F14的闪燃理论** → CH12整段弃船场景 → CH14"威胁只持续几秒"的论点。如果F14这个2026年理论后续被推翻或只是多种假说之一，CH12的叙事就从"合理推测"变成"误导性虚构"。

- **桶数矛盾**：CH03说"1,701 barrels"，CH09说"1,700 barrels"，相差1桶。后续所有提到桶数的地方（CH11货舱气味、CH12爆炸）都依赖这个基数。

- **距离数据**：F15说"最后日志显示距Santa Maria约6-110海里（来源有差异）"，CH10选了"110 miles"，但如果真实距离是6海里，"九天后在400海里外被发现"意味着船漂了394海里，这个漂移速度是否合理？会影响"他们能否追上船"的判断。
factcheck.report:
# 事实核验报告

## 一、致命风险

### [F14] 货舱爆炸场景的叙事性质

**原文主张**：CH12 整段用第一人称现在时写成主角亲历的确定事实："A sound. Like a heavy door slamming. Then a boom. The hatch to the cargo hold—it flies open... A flash... Captain Briggs: 'All hands! Abandon ship! Now!'"

**核验结果**：
- R1（PerthNow 2026-05-22）：University of Manchester 专家 "claim to have finally worked out what **may have happened**"，Rowbotham "**suggest**ed alcohol vapours... **could have caused** an explosion"
- R2（Marine Insight 2026-05-21）：虽用"proven explanation"，但实际是"1:18 比例**模型实验**"推导；"Findings later revealed that the 9 wooden barrels had leaked"是事后检查发现，不是当时的目击
- R6（东方日报 2026-05-19）："1比18比例的商船模型**試驗**表明船艙內乙醇蒸氣積聚，**可能**引發威力巨大的爆炸"
- R4, R21 等多个来源确认：船被发现时**无人生还**（"no one aboard", "todos sus ocupantes habían desaparecido"），没有任何目击者证词

**证据来源**：R1, R2, R6（2026年学术研究）；R4, R21（无幸存者的历史事实）  
**证据等级**：E - 文案写法与证据矛盾：闪燃理论是2026年模型实验推导的假说，不是1872年的历史记录或目击证词  
**风险级别**：致命 - 观众会误以为CH12的感官细节（"like a heavy door slamming", "Captain Briggs: 'All hands!'"）是历史记录，但实际上没有任何幸存者，所有对话和声音描写都是虚构的  
**处理方式**：标明估算 - CH12前必须加明确标注："What you're about to see is a **reconstruction based on a 2026 University of Manchester study**. No one survived to tell us what actually happened. This is what the science suggests **may have** occurred." 且CH12内的对话改为间接叙述："The captain must have given the order. We must have grabbed what we could." 不要写具体对话内容

---

## 二、高风险

### [F06] 7.7% 存活率的口径问题

**原文主张**：CH13 "That's a 7.7% survival rate. That's what 'open lifeboat, December Atlantic' **actually means**" 用单一案例的结果暗示这是该环境的标准死亡率

**核验结果**：
- R7-R12 确认 John Rutledge 1856 年案例：13人，9天，1人存活
- 独立计算：1 ÷ 13 = 7.692... % ≈ 7.7%（计算正确）
- 但搜索结果中**没有**"19世纪大西洋冬季救生艇事故统计数据"
- 这是**单一案例**的个案结果，不是统计学意义上的期望存活率

**证据来源**：R7-R12（John Rutledge案例）  
**证据等级**：C - 数字本身正确，但口径不匹配：这是一个案例，不是该环境的统计规律  
**风险级别**：高 - "actually means" 的措辞让观众以为这是统计数据  
**处理方式**：限定表述 - "In 1856, same waters, same season, 13 people got into a lifeboat. Nine days. One survived. One out of thirteen." 删除 "That's what it actually means" 这种泛化表达，让观众自己推断这个案例的代表性

### [F12] 船员报酬与crimp费用

**原文主张**：CH01 "Forty dollars for the voyage—except that's his fee, not my pay. I just signed on to cross the Atlantic **for free**" 暗示$40是全部报酬且全被crimp扣光

**核验结果**：
- R15（Nautical Magazine 1871）：crimp费用 "from **eight shillings to ten shillings per head**"（约$2-3美元，按1870s汇率粗算）
- R13-R14 讨论了crimp系统和工资，但没有给出"$40全是crimp费用"或"2-3个月工资作介绍费"的直接数字
- F12 提到的 "$40 crimp费用" 与 R15 的 "8-10先令" 数量级不符

**证据来源**：R15（crimp费用范围）  
**证据等级**：D - 有crimp系统的描述，但没有直接支持"$40全被扣"或"for free"的证据  
**风险级别**：高 - 如果$40是典型航程工资而crimp费用约$2-3，"for free"就是夸大  
**处理方式**：删除具体数字 - "The crimp at the docks found me work. He takes his cut upfront—most of what I'd make this voyage. I'm crossing the Atlantic for almost nothing." 不说"$40"或"for free"

---

## 三、中风险

### [F07] 9天 vs 10天

**原文主张**：CH01, CH10 多处写 "in nine days" "Nine days from now"

**核验结果**：
- R22（Britannica）："The British brig Dei Gratia spotted the Mary Celeste **ten days** after the last log entry, dated November 25"
- R24（Times of India）：发现日期 "December 4, 1872"
- R23（Papers Past）：发现日期 "December 5, 1872"
- 独立计算：
  - 11月25日 → 12月4日 = 9天
  - 11月25日 → 12月5日 = 10天
  - Britannica明确说"ten days"

**证据来源**：R22, R23, R24  
**证据等级**：B - Britannica（可靠来源）说10天，但发现日期有12月4日/5日两种说法  
**风险级别**：中 - 差一天对论点影响不大，但与Britannica不一致  
**处理方式**：修正数字 - 改为 "About ten days from now" 或 "In nine or ten days"

### [F02] 船长妻子名字

**原文主张**：CH01等多处写 "His wife Sarah"，F02标注"一些来源称Sophia存在争议"

**核验结果**：
- R16（ABC Radio 2015）："his wife, **Sarah**, their two year-old daughter, **Sophia**"
- R17（Peabody Essex Museum档案）："Capt. Benjamin Briggs's wife, **Sarah Cobb Briggs**"
- R21, R28, R29：都确认妻子Sarah，女儿Sophia
- 搜索结果中**没有**找到"妻子名叫Sophia"的来源

**证据来源**：R16, R17, R21, R28, R29  
**证据等级**：A - 原始档案（R17）和多个来源都确认妻子是Sarah Cobb Briggs  
**风险级别**：无 - 文案正确，F02标注可能有误（Sophia是女儿）  
**处理方式**：保留

### [F01] 目的港Genoa

**原文主张**：CH01 "a voyage to Italy" / "until we reach Genoa"

**核验结果**：
- R20（Britannica）："destined for **Genoa, Italy**"
- R21（ABC Radio）："bound for **Genoa, Italy**"
- R31（RRI.co.id）："tujuan mereka, **Genoa, Italia**"

**证据来源**：R20, R21, R31  
**证据等级**：A  
**处理方式**：保留

### [F05] John Rutledge案例所有细节

**原文主张**：CH13 "1856. John Rutledge. Liverpool to New York. Same waters. Same season. The ship went down. Thirteen people got into a lifeboat. They drifted for nine days. One person survived."

**核验结果**：
- R7（Stanford University）：书籍《Adrift》记录 "Liverpool-to-New York trip in the **early months of 1856**"，"five lifeboats were lowered"，"the last boat... **thirteen souls. Only one would survive**"，"**nine days adrift** more than **four hundred miles off Newfoundland**"
- R11, R12, R34-R36：多个出版记录确认同样细节

**证据来源**：R7, R11, R12（书籍《Adrift》by Brian Murphy）  
**证据等级**：A  
**处理方式**：保留

---

## 四、低风险（观众不易察觉，保留）

### [F03] 补给"足够两次"

**原文**：CH09 "Hardtack enough to reach Genoa twice over"  
**核验**：R4, R5, R21 确认"provisiones"/"cargo intact"，但没有"两次"的量化  
**证据等级**：D  
**风险**：低 - 修辞性夸张，观众不会核实具体吨位  
**处理**：保留（观众不易察觉，核心论点"有充足补给"成立）

### [F13] 船员配给标准

**原文**：CH05 "six pounds of bread per week, a pound and a half of salted beef per day"  
**核验**：搜索结果未找到1870s商船标准配给数字  
**证据等级**：D  
**风险**：低 - 背景细节，观众不会查证  
**处理**：保留（观众不易察觉，属于合理历史重建）

### [F11] 救生艇类型yawl

**原文**：CH12 "The yawl's being lowered"  
**核验**：R23确认"only one boat"失踪，但未说明型号  
**证据等级**：D  
**风险**：低 - "yawl"是19世纪商船常见类型，且"open boat"是关键  
**处理**：保留（观众不易察觉，型号名称不影响"开放式+无动力"的论点）

---

## 五、已证实错误/不足的汇总

### 已证实错误的数字
1. **"Nine days"应为"Ten days"或"Nine or ten days"**（F07，Britannica明确说ten days）

### 已证实错误的事实
1. **CH12的叙事方式**：将2026年模型实验假说写成1872年亲历事实，且包含虚构对话

### 证据不足的关键结论
1. **7.7%作为环境标准死亡率**（F06）：只有一个案例，不是统计规律
2. **$40报酬全被crimp扣光**（F12）：搜索结果显示crimp费用约8-10先令（$2-3），不是$40

### 需要改的绝对化表达
1. CH13 "That's what 'open lifeboat, December Atlantic' **actually means**" → 删除"actually means"，改为只陈述案例
2. CH01 "for free" → 改为"for almost nothing"

### 可能影响全文结论的计算依赖链
- 无。核心论点"弃船决定比留船更致命"不依赖精确的9天/10天，也不依赖7.7%是否为统计数据（一个真实案例足以说明危险性）

### 发布前必须人工决定的事项

1. **CH12叙事合法性**：即使CH02已声明"We don't know exactly what happened"，后面用第一人称现在时详细重演爆炸（"A sound. Like a heavy door slamming. Then a boom."）+虚构船长对话（"All hands! Abandon ship! Now!"），观众能否区分这是"基于理论的重演"而非"历史事实"？是否需要在CH12开始前再次明确标注"This is a **reconstruction based on 2026 research**, not historical record"？

2. **闪燃理论的确定性程度**：R2虽用"proven explanation"（媒体用语），但学术上仍是"最可能假说"（R1: "may have", "could have"；R6: "可能"）。稿子应在哪个位置标注理论的不确定性？还是认为"leading scientific theory"已足够可信？

3. **单一案例的代表性**：用John Rutledge一个案例说明"开放救生艇+冬季大西洋+400海里"的致命性，在叙事上是否可接受？还是必须明说"We only have one documented case, but..."？从留存角度看，"13人仅1人活"已足够震撼，是否需要弱化它的代表性？

---

history.text:
I'm a sailor on the Mary Celeste. It's November 1872, and I just signed on for a voyage to Italy. The ship is solid, the cargo is valuable, and the captain brought his wife and daughter. Everything seems fine. Except I know something no one else on this ship knows: in nine days, we're all going to be dead. Not because of a storm, not because of pirates. Because of a lifeboat.

How did I end up here? A crimp at the docks found me work. Forty dollars for the voyage—except that's his fee, not my pay. I just signed on to cross the Atlantic for free.

There are ten of us on this ship. Captain Benjamin Briggs. His wife Sarah. Their two-year-old daughter. Seven crew. In a few days, this ship will be found drifting 400 miles from land. Empty. No bodies. No struggle.

Why would ten people abandon a perfectly good ship?

I need to get into the captain's cabin. Find the ship's log, the charts—anything that explains what happens next.

So what's my mission?

Three places. The captain's cabin—that's where the log is, the navigation charts, the decisions. The cargo hold—1,701 barrels of industrial alcohol down there. And the deck—where we work, where we'll be when it happens.

Ten people on this ship. Captain Briggs. His wife Sarah. Their two-year-old daughter. Seven crew, including me.

The ship's sound. Cargo's secured. Supplies are good.

So why does everyone abandon it?

That's what I need to find out. When did they decide? What made them think: we have to leave right now?

Because that decision—that one choice—kills all of us.

All right. Let's start where I sleep.

November 25th.

That's the last time anyone writes a date in the log.

Ship's position: about 110 miles west of Santa Maria Island, Azores.

Nine days from now, this ship will be found drifting 400 miles out. Empty.

You don't know which day. You don't know which hour.

But somewhere in these nine days, all ten people on this ship—Captain Briggs, his wife Sarah, his two-year-old daughter, every crew member, me—

We're going to see something. Or hear something.

Something that makes all of us think: we have to leave this ship. Right now.

And that decision—that one decision in the next nine days—

Is going to kill every single one of us.

I don't know when it's coming.

But I know it's coming.

Over the next few days, I notice something.

Down near the cargo hold. This smell. Alcohol. Sharp. Strong. Way stronger than it should be.

I mention it to one of the other hands. He shrugs. "It's 1,700 barrels. Of course it smells."

But it doesn't sit right.

I go to the first mate. "Sir, the cargo hold. The alcohol smell. It's unusually strong."

He looks at me, tired. "Cargo settling. Happens every time we carry spirits. Barrels shift, vapor escapes. Normal."

"But sir—"

"Son, you're what, two years at sea? I've been sailing fifteen. I know what normal smells like. Get back to your watch."

Two days later I catch Captain Briggs on deck. "Captain, I think there's something wrong with—"

"The cargo smell. The mate told me you were concerned." He's calm. "I checked the hold myself. Nine barrels empty, we knew that loading. The rest are secure. No leaks. The smell is strong because we're in warmer waters. The vapor expands. It's chemistry, not danger. I appreciate your vigilance, but trust my judgment here."

I'm a crew member. Not an officer. Not in the decision room.

I tried.

But what I think doesn't carry weight.

I don't know what day it is. Maybe morning, maybe night.

But I'm on deck when it happens.

A sound. Like a heavy door slamming. Then a boom.

The hatch to the cargo hold—it flies open. The force sends the cover crashing onto the deck.

The smell. Alcohol. Thick. Sharp.

A flash—something bright down in the hold. Just for a second. Then gone.

But Captain Briggs is already moving.

"All hands! Abandon ship! Now!"

He's running to his quarters. Comes back carrying his daughter. She's two years old, half asleep. Sarah's right behind him.

We grab what we can. The yawl's being lowered.

Ten of us. Into an open boat.

Captain Briggs: "Row. Away from the ship."

We row.

I look back. The Mary Celeste is still there. Floating. Intact. No fire. No smoke. The sails are up. The rigging is fine.

Everything we need—food, water, shelter—it's all still on that ship.

But we're here. Four hundred miles from land. December. Atlantic Ocean. An open yawl. No engine. Just oars.

Exposed to wind. Cold. Waves.

Remember what Old Thomas said? "Trust the ship. She'll tell you if she's dying."

And right now—in this moment—the ship is telling us: I'm fine. The explosion's over. Stay.

But none of us are listening.

We're rowing away from the only safe place we have.

There's one more thing you need to know.

1856. John Rutledge. Liverpool to New York. Same waters. Same season.

The ship went down. Thirteen people got into a lifeboat. They drifted for nine days.

One person survived. One.

Thirteen people. Nine days. One survivor.

We have ten in this boat. One of them is a two-year-old child. A two-year-old.

Four hundred miles from land. Open boat. Winter storm.

That's a 7.7% survival rate. That's what "open lifeboat, December Atlantic" actually means.

Not "we'll row to shore." Not "someone will find us."

Hypothermia. Dehydration. Exposure.

The ship we just left—it's intact. The hull is sound. There's food. Water. Shelter from wind.

Everything we need to survive for months.

And we chose this.

I can't—I can't watch this anymore.

You read about the Mary Celeste, you think: what did they encounter?

Living it, you know.

They encountered something that looked terrifying for a few seconds—a flash, a bang, the smell of alcohol, maybe fire.

But it was already over. What they ran from—that flash, that noise—it lasted seconds. No sustained flame. No structural damage. The ship was fine.

What they jumped into—400 miles from land, winter Atlantic, an open boat—that was the actual death sentence.

Next time you're under pressure to make a decision right now—to quit, to leave, to sell—stop for three seconds and ask yourself:

Is this threat going to keep getting worse, or is it just terrifying for this one moment?

And the exit I'm about to take—is it actually safer than staying where I am?

Because ten people on the Mary Celeste, including a two-year-old girl, got that judgment wrong in those three seconds.

And that's why the ship was found intact. And they weren't.
